real.summary: Eighteen papers were named in the study, and the 16 whose haunted version is still on arXiv were all caught, each one recognised as talking to an AI, even the ones written in 0.1 pt type that no screen can draw. The other two were withdrawn before I could check them. One paper also has a table title printed white on a dark band that pdf.js reads as inkless, so it shows up as a second hidden line that says nothing to an AI, and the page lists it below the real ghost.

planted.summary: I hid one instruction in a research abstract, a résumé and a student essay in each of eight ways, plus seven in three web pages, and every one was found and recognised, while the four honest copies, which keep white text on dark bands on purpose, raised nothing. The one trick I left out of the score is a sentence laced with zero-width characters so that keyword filters miss it, because it is printed in plain sight and a person can read it too.

clean.summary: Not one of the 38 papers posted to arXiv this week was flagged as talking to an AI. Six do carry longer hidden text, mostly labels drawn over images and lines pdf.js places outside the page, and the tool lists those quietly under a calm verdict, while 24 have the short fragments it only counts, like figure labels and maths symbols on coloured boxes.

gemma.summary: Gemma 3 1B read the start of each real paper as a peer reviewer, once the way an AI receives it and once with the hidden text taken out, and on all 16 the hidden sentence pushed its chance of answering Accept to between 98.5% and 100%, up from a median of 30% without it. It reads about the first thousand characters, which is all that fits in a graphics card in one pass, so when the hidden sentence sits later in the paper it is added after that opening, and the exorcised copy is read over the same opening without it.
